label: Digitally Immersed & Emotionally Strained
summary: This profile represents highly educated women who spend substantial time on social media (averaging nearly 4 hours daily, with many exceeding 5 hours) and report elevated levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety. Across all three psychological distress measures—loneliness (UCLA-8), depression (PHQ-9), and anxiety (GAD-7)—their scores are consistently in the higher range, with anxiety symptoms being particularly pronounced. The combination of heavy social-media engagement and heightened emotional distress distinguishes this group from lower-use, lower-distress profiles.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, daily social-media use exceeding 5 hours
behavior_markers: Heavy daily social-media usage averaging approximately 3.9 hours with a substantial proportion exceeding 5 hours
Elevated loneliness scores (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.78) indicating persistent feelings of social disconnection
Moderate-to-high depressive symptom burden (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 1.81)
Notably high anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 mean ≈ 2.27), the most pronounced distress indicator in this profile
Co-occurrence of all three psychological distress dimensions alongside intensive digital social engagement
tone: Concerned and empathetic, reflecting the convergence of significant emotional distress with heavy digital engagement in a highly educated female cohort

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents male respondents with graduate-level education who report notably low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms. Their daily social media use is relatively light, averaging roughly 2.8 hours per day (within the 1–3 hour bracket). Across all psychological well-being indicators, this group scores well below scale midpoints, suggesting generally positive mental health and moderate digital engagement.
demographic_anchor: Male, graduate degree or above, 1–3 hours of daily social media use
behavior_markers: Low loneliness scores (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 0.78, well below scale midpoint)
Minimal depressive symptomatology (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 0.27, near floor)
Very low anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 mean ≈ 0.03, near floor)
Light daily social media consumption averaging approximately 2.8 hours
Consistent pattern of psychological well-being across all measured dimensions

label: Lonely but Low-Distress Heavy Social-Media User
summary: This profile captures highly educated women who report elevated loneliness despite relatively low levels of depressive and anxiety symptoms. They spend nearly 5 hours per day on social media, suggesting that heavy online engagement may coexist with—or serve as a compensatory response to—perceived social disconnection, rather than being driven by clinical-level mood or anxiety disturbance.
demographic_anchor: Female, graduate-level education or above, 3–5 hours of daily social-media use
behavior_markers: Elevated loneliness scores (UCLA-8 mean ≈ 1.30) indicating moderate perceived social isolation
Below-average depressive symptom severity (PHQ-9 mean ≈ 0.90)
Below-average anxiety symptom severity (GAD-7 mean ≈ 0.85)
Heavy daily social-media use averaging approximately 4.9 hours
Possible use of social media as a substitute for in-person social connection
tone: Socially disconnected yet emotionally stable; quietly seeking connection online without overt psychological distress

label: Well-Adjusted Light-Use Graduate Male
summary: This profile represents a group of highly educated males who report notably low levels of loneliness, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms, paired with relatively light daily social-media use averaging roughly 1.6 hours. With a UCLA-8 loneliness mean of approximately 1.22, PHQ-9 depression mean of about 0.82, and GAD-7 anxiety mean near 0.90, these respondents consistently score well below clinical concern thresholds across all three psychological well-being measures. Their moderate, bounded engagement with social media (typically 1–3 hours per day) suggests a disciplined or purposeful usage pattern rather than habitual or excessive scrolling.
demographic_anchor: Male, holding a graduate degree or above, reporting 1–3 hours of daily social-media use
behavior_markers: Light daily social-media use averaging approximately 1.6 hours
Consistently low self-reported loneliness scores (UCLA-8 mean ~1.22)
Minimal depressive symptomatology (PHQ-9 mean ~0.82)
Low anxiety symptomatology (GAD-7 mean ~0.90)
Bounded and moderate engagement with social-media platforms rather than heavy or compulsive use
